claim: Interactions between the thalamus and cortex are essential for sensory processing.
source: Interactions between the thalamus and cortex are essential for sensory processing (Lien and Scanziani, 2018; Bartlett, 2013), motor control (Fresno et al., 2019; Guo et al., 2017), arousal (Chen et al., 2015; Schiff, 2008) and multiple aspects of cognitive function (Wimmer et al., 2015; Wolff and Vann, 2019; Jaramillo et al., 2019; Parnaudeau et al., 2018; Pergola et al., 2018; Rikhye et al., 2018a; Saalmann and Kastner, 2011; Bolkan et al., 2017; Scott et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The thalamus is primarily composed of excitatory neurons that are devoid of recurrent local connections.
source: The thalamus is primarily composed of excitatory neurons that are devoid of recurrent local connections, giving way to the notion that the computations thalamic microcircuits perform will have to rely on dynamic changes in their inputs (Halassa and Kastner, 2017; Jaramillo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about thalamic anatomy supported by citations.

claim: The computations thalamic microcircuits perform will have to rely on dynamic changes in their inputs.
source: The thalamus is primarily composed of excitatory neurons that are devoid of recurrent local connections, giving way to the notion that the computations thalamic microcircuits perform will have to rely on dynamic changes in their inputs (Halassa and Kastner, 2017; Jaramillo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference about thalamic computation based on anatomical structure, supported by citations.

claim: Lateral geniculate thalamic neurons receive strong and orderly segregated inputs from subcortical sources.
source: In early sensory pathways such as the geniculocortical, lateral geniculate thalamic neurons receive strong and orderly segregated inputs from subcortical sources (Hubel and Wiesel, 1961; Usrey et al., 1999), making their responses similar to their inputs (but see Liang et al., 2018), and suggesting a relatively limited computational role (Lien and Scanziani, 2013; Priebe and Ferster, 2012; Reid and Alonso, 1996; Li et al., 2013b; Li et al., 2013a).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Lateral geniculate thalamic neuron responses are similar to their inputs.
source: In early sensory pathways such as the geniculocortical, lateral geniculate thalamic neurons receive strong and orderly segregated inputs from subcortical sources (Hubel and Wiesel, 1961; Usrey et al., 1999), making their responses similar to their inputs (but see Liang et al., 2018), and suggesting a relatively limited computational role (Lien and Scanziani, 2013; Priebe and Ferster, 2012; Reid and Alonso, 1996; Li et al., 2013b; Li et al., 2013a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations, with a caveat noted.

claim: Lateral geniculate thalamic neurons have a relatively limited computational role.
source: In early sensory pathways such as the geniculocortical, lateral geniculate thalamic neurons receive strong and orderly segregated inputs from subcortical sources (Hubel and Wiesel, 1961; Usrey et al., 1999), making their responses similar to their inputs (but see Liang et al., 2018), and suggesting a relatively limited computational role (Lien and Scanziani, 2013; Priebe and Ferster, 2012; Reid and Alonso, 1996; Li et al., 2013b; Li et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cortical neurons in primary cortical areas show sensory responses that are qualitatively distinct but explained by a weighted sum of the thalamic inputs they receive.
source: In fact, because cortical neurons in primary cortical areas show sensory responses that are qualitatively distinct but explained by a weighted sum of the thalamic inputs they receive (Finn et al., 2007; Alonso et al., 2007; Lien and Scanziani, 2013; Usrey and Alitto, 2015), the sensory thalamic microcircuits are thought to function primarily as relays (Guillery and Sherman, 2002; Sherman, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Sensory thalamic microcircuits are thought to function primarily as relays.
source: In fact, because cortical neurons in primary cortical areas show sensory responses that are qualitatively distinct but explained by a weighted sum of the thalamic inputs they receive (Finn et al., 2007; Alonso et al., 2007; Lien and Scanziani, 2013; Usrey and Alitto, 2015), the sensory thalamic microcircuits are thought to function primarily as relays (Guillery and Sherman, 2002; Sherman, 2016).
evidence: This is a conceptual interpretation supported by citations.

claim: The notion that the thalamus is largely a relay station permeates the literature on thalamocortical interactions.
source: Despite the paucity of data on thalamic microcircuit structural organization beyond these select sensory pathways, the notion that the thalamus is largely a relay station permeates the literature on thalamocortical interactions (Mitchell, 2015; Moustafa et al., 2017; Sherman, 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature, supported by citations.

claim: There is a paucity of data on thalamic microcircuit structural organization beyond select sensory pathways.
source: Despite the paucity of data on thalamic microcircuit structural organization beyond these select sensory pathways, the notion that the thalamus is largely a relay station permeates the literature on thalamocortical interactions (Mitchell, 2015; Moustafa et al., 2017; Sherman, 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about the knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Neurons in the posterior Pulvinar nuclear complex or the Mediodorsal nucleus have been hypothesized to operate as higher order relays.
source: For example, neurons in areas like the posterior Pulvinar nuclear complex or the Mediodorsal nucleus, which constitutes a large part of the human thalamus (Chalfin et al., 2007) have been hypothesized to operate as higher order relays, transmitting signals from one cortical area to another.
evidence: This is a statement about existing hypotheses in the literature, supported by a citation.

claim: The Mediodorsal nucleus constitutes a large part of the human thalamus.
source: For example, neurons in areas like the posterior Pulvinar nuclear complex or the Mediodorsal nucleus, which constitutes a large part of the human thalamus (Chalfin et al., 2007) have been hypothesized to operate as higher order relays, transmitting signals from one cortical area to another.
evidence: This is an anatomical fact supported by a citation.

claim: There is some experimental support for the higher order relay hypothesis.
source: Although there is some experimental support for this idea (Guillery and Sherman, 2002; Sherman, 2016; Sherman and Guillery, 2002), whether the higher order relay function is universal, or describes only a subset of the computations carried out in these nuclei is an open question.
evidence: This statement acknowledges existing evidence while noting uncertainty, supported by citations.

claim: Whether the higher order relay function is universal, or describes only a subset of the computations carried out in these nuclei is an open question.
source: Although there is some experimental support for this idea (Guillery and Sherman, 2002; Sherman, 2016; Sherman and Guillery, 2002), whether the higher order relay function is universal, or describes only a subset of the computations carried out in these nuclei is an open question.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Certain responses in the pulvinar and posterior nucleus may be explained by convergent cortical and/or subcortical inputs.
source: In fact, a number of functional studies suggest that certain responses in the pulvinar and posterior nucleus maybe explained by convergent cortical and/or subcortical inputs (Groh et al., 2014; Komura et al., 2013; Roth et al., 2016), indicating that at least some of these microcircuits may be performing computations on their inputs (Bieler et al., 2018; Mease et al., 2017; Whitmire et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to functional studies.

claim: At least some of these microcircuits may be performing computations on their inputs.
source: In fact, a number of functional studies suggest that certain responses in the pulvinar and posterior nucleus maybe explained by convergent cortical and/or subcortical inputs (Groh et al., 2014; Komura et al., 2013; Roth et al., 2016), indicating that at least some of these microcircuits may be performing computations on their inputs (Bieler et al., 2018; Mease et al., 2017; Whitmire et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation of functional studies, supported by citations.

claim: Pulvinar neurons may be preferentially innervating inhibitory neurons in primary visual cortex, contributing to surround suppression of their sensory responses.
source: In addition, a recent study in the mouse has shown that pulvinar neurons may be preferentially innervating inhibitory neurons in primary visual cortex, contributing to surround suppression of their sensory responses (Fang et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: These studies challenge the notion of these nuclei functioning uniformly as higher order relays.
source: Together, these studies challenge the notion of these nuclei functioning uniformly as higher order relays.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cited studies.

claim: A number of open questions exist regarding the wiring diversity of thalamic microcircuits and the computations that they perform.
source: More generally, a number of open questions exist regarding the wiring diversity of thalamic microcircuits and the computations that they perform (Halassa and Sherman, 2019; Nakajima and Halassa, 2017).
evidence: This statement identifies knowledge gaps, supported by citations.

claim: Thalamocortical neurons in the ventromedial thalamus are engaged in maintaining preparatory motor activity in premotor cortex of the mouse.
source: For example, thalamocortical neurons in the ventromedial thalamus are engaged in maintaining preparatory motor activity in premotor cortex of the mouse (Guo et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: A speed control function in regulating cortical preparatory dynamics has been described for the ventroanterior/ventrolateral thalamus in primates.
source: In primates, a speed control function in regulating cortical preparatory dynamics has been described for the ventroanterior/ventrolateral thalamus (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: These types of functions are much better described from a control theory perspective, where the thalamus constrains cortical dynamics rather than transmit signals as in early sensory systems.
source: These types of functions are much better described from a control theory perspective (Kao et al., 2020), where the thalamus constrains cortical dynamics rather than transmit signals as in early sensory systems (Nakajima and Halassa, 2017).
evidence: This is a conceptual interpretation supported by citations.

claim: The mediodorsal thalamus (MD) is the largest thalamic input to the prefrontal cortex (PFC).
source: For example, the mediodorsal thalamus (MD), the largest thalamic input to the prefrontal cortex (PFC) has been shown to be critical for maintaining cognitive control signals underlying attention (Schmitt et al., 2017), adaptive decision making (Alcaraz et al., 2018) and working memory (Bolkan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an anatomical fact stated in the context of functional studies.

claim: The mediodorsal thalamus has been shown to be critical for maintaining cognitive control signals underlying attention.
source: For example, the mediodorsal thalamus (MD), the largest thalamic input to the prefrontal cortex (PFC) has been shown to be critical for maintaining cognitive control signals underlying attention (Schmitt et al., 2017), adaptive decision making (Alcaraz et al., 2018) and working memory (Bolkan et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: The mediodorsal thalamus has been shown to be critical for adaptive decision making.
source: For example, the mediodorsal thalamus (MD), the largest thalamic input to the prefrontal cortex (PFC) has been shown to be critical for maintaining cognitive control signals underlying attention (Schmitt et al., 2017), adaptive decision making (Alcaraz et al., 2018) and working memory (Bolkan et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: The mediodorsal thalamus has been shown to be critical for working memory.
source: For example, the mediodorsal thalamus (MD), the largest thalamic input to the prefrontal cortex (PFC) has been shown to be critical for maintaining cognitive control signals underlying attention (Schmitt et al., 2017), adaptive decision making (Alcaraz et al., 2018) and working memory (Bolkan et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: The mediodorsal thalamus is critical for enabling animals to flexibly switch between different rules that guide behavioral choice.
source: In addition, this thalamic structure is also critical for enabling animals to flexibly switch between different rules that guide behavioral choice (Rikhye et al., 2018a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: The MD thalamus contains a functional subpopulation that exerts a suppressive impact on prefrontal activity, enabling its representations to switch according to shifts in behavioral context.
source: One study (Rikhye et al., 2018a) has shown that the MD thalamus contains a functional subpopulation that exerts a suppressive impact on prefrontal activity, enabling its representations to switch according to shifts in behavioral context.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: The anatomical circuit substrates underlying MD suppressive functionality are poorly understood.
source: The anatomical circuit substrates underlying such functionality are poorly understood.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that motivates the current study.

claim: The prelimbic part of the PFC (PL) is a hypothesized rodent analogue of primate dorsolateral PFC.
source: Motivated by these functional studies, we examined in mice the reciprocal connectivity of MD neurons with their targets in the prelimbic part of the PFC (PL), a hypothesized rodent analogue of primate dorsolateral PFC (Hoover and Vertes, 2007; Vertes, 2004).
evidence: This is a statement about anatomical homology supported by citations.

claim: The MD→PL thalamocortical loop engages in a variety of cognitive control, non-relay functions.
source: Given the notion that this thalamocortical loop engages in a variety of cognitive control, non-relay functions (Ferguson and Gao, 2018; Schmitt and Halassa, 2017), we systematically compared the impact of MD activation on PL activity, as well as its input/output connectivity patterns to those of a classical sensory one.
evidence: This is a statement about the functional role of the MD→PL loop, supported by citations.

claim: Sustained drive of MD neurons broadly over several hundred milliseconds using SSFOs resulted in prelimbic activity patterns that were dominated by inhibition.
source: Sustained drive of MD neurons broadly over several hundred milliseconds, using stabilized step-function opsins (SSFOs), resulted in prelimbic activity patterns that were dominated by inhibition.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study, supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: Equivalent manipulation of the MGB resulted in robust A1 excitatory drive.
source: This was quite distinct from an equivalent manipulation of the MGB, where A1 excitatory drive was robust.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study, supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: The functional differences between MD→PL and MGB→A1 were explained by a series of anatomical findings including unique patterns of excitatory/inhibitory cortical innervation across the two loops.
source: These functional differences were explained by a series of anatomical findings including unique patterns of excitatory/inhibitory cortical innervation across the two loops.
evidence: This is an interpretation linking anatomical findings to functional observations.

claim: The medial geniculate body (MGB) innervated excitatory A1 neurons in higher proportions compared to the manner by which MD terminals innervated PL microcircuits.
source: More specifically, the medial geniculate body (MGB) innervated excitatory A1 neurons in higher proportions compared to the manner by which MD terminals innervated PL microcircuits.
evidence: This is an anatomical finding from the study, supported by data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: There is a striking difference in the size of MD vs. MGB synaptic terminals selectively labeled using BDA.
source: In addition, we observed a striking difference in the size of MD vs. MGB synaptic terminals selectively labeled using BDA as well as genetic labeling using mammalian green fluorescence protein [GFP] reconstitution across synaptic partners (mGRASP Feng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an anatomical finding from the study, supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: There is a striking difference in the size of MD vs. MGB synaptic terminals selectively labeled using mGRASP.
source: In addition, we observed a striking difference in the size of MD vs. MGB synaptic terminals selectively labeled using BDA as well as genetic labeling using mammalian green fluorescence protein [GFP] reconstitution across synaptic partners (mGRASP Feng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an anatomical finding from the study, supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: The major excitatory inputs to the MD are from frontal cortical areas.
source: In addition to these output structural differences, we also saw difference on the input side, where the major excitatory inputs to the MD are from frontal cortical areas, compared to MGB that receives excitatory drive mostly from the midbrain.
evidence: This is an anatomical finding from the study, supported by data in Figures 5-7.

claim: The MGB receives excitatory drive mostly from the midbrain.
source: In addition to these output structural differences, we also saw difference on the input side, where the major excitatory inputs to the MD are from frontal cortical areas, compared to MGB that receives excitatory drive mostly from the midbrain.
evidence: This is an anatomical finding from the study, supported by data in Figures 5-7.

claim: Based on the origin of their driving inputs, the data is consistent with the notion of the MD as a higher order nucleus and the MGB as a first order nucleus.
source: Based on the origin of their driving inputs our data is consistent with the notion of the MD as a higher order nucleus and the MGB as a first order nucleus (Mitchell, 2015; Sherman and Guillery, 1998).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data in the context of existing classification schemes, supported by citations.

claim: The findings are in line with the broader notion of sensory thalamus being modulated by its cortical target, while associative thalamus being driven by its cortical target.
source: They are also in line with the broader notion of sensory thalamus being modulated by its cortical target, while associative thalamus being driven by its cortical target (Crick and Koch, 1998).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data in the context of existing theories, supported by a citation.

claim: The study provides structural and functional explanation for why some thalamocortical loops perform a relay function, while others are more suited for integrative and cognitive control functions.
source: Overall, our study provides structural and functional explanation for why some thalamocortical loops perform a relay function, while others are more suited for integrative and cognitive control functions.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: MD and MGB were transduced with stabilized step function opsins (SSFO) to uniformly enhance excitability.
source: We sought to uniformly enhance excitability in either the MD or MGB, akin to a step current injection. Therefore, in two groups of animals (N = 5 animals per condition), we transduced either the MD (Figure 1A) or MGB (Figure 1B) with stabilized step function opsins (SSFO, hChR2(C128S/D156A)), an optical actuator known to precisely accomplish this goal (Yizhar et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used, supported by a citation.

claim: The lateral MD was preferentially targeted because this area is known to primarily target the PL.
source: Using stereotactic injections (see Materials and methods), we preferentially targeted the lateral MD and the ventral portion of the MGB, because these areas are known to primarily target the PL (Groenewegen, 1988) and A1 (Winer et al., 2005), respectively.
evidence: This describes the experimental targeting strategy, supported by citations.

claim: The ventral portion of the MGB was preferentially targeted because this area is known to primarily target A1.
source: Using stereotactic injections (see Materials and methods), we preferentially targeted the lateral MD and the ventral portion of the MGB, because these areas are known to primarily target the PL (Groenewegen, 1988) and A1 (Winer et al., 2005), respectively.
evidence: This describes the experimental targeting strategy, supported by citations.

claim: Optical stimulation resulted in comparable increase in thalamic spiking across MD and MGB (MD = 66.18 +/- 1.89%, MGB = 67.06 +/- 3.83%).
source: Across each animal, we ensured that optical stimulation resulted in comparable increase in thalamic spiking (spiking enhancement: MD = 66.18 +/- 1.89% (mean +/- SEM; n = 298 neurons), MGB = 67.06 +/- 3.83% (mean +/- SEM; n = 597 neurons); Figure 1D; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental result shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In the PL, MD activation suppressed the spike rate of RS neurons.
source: Specifically, in the PL, MD activation suppressed the spike rate of RS neurons and predominantly enhanced FS neural spiking (n = 441 RS, 265 FS neurons; group averages: Figure 1E–H, Figure 1—source data 1; individual animals: Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figures 1E-H.

claim: In the PL, MD activation predominantly enhanced FS neural spiking.
source: Specifically, in the PL, MD activation suppressed the spike rate of RS neurons and predominantly enhanced FS neural spiking (n = 441 RS, 265 FS neurons; group averages: Figure 1E–H, Figure 1—source data 1; individual animals: Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figures 1E-H.

claim: MGB activation robustly drove A1 RS neurons.
source: In contrast, MGB activation robustly drove A1 RS neurons with variable effects on FS neurons (i.e. both excitatory and inhibitory effects were observed with similar proportions, n = 724 RS, 191 FS neurons; Figure 1E–H, Figure 1—source data 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figures 1E-H.

claim: MGB activation had variable effects on A1 FS neurons (both excitatory and inhibitory effects were observed with similar proportions).
source: In contrast, MGB activation robustly drove A1 RS neurons with variable effects on FS neurons (i.e. both excitatory and inhibitory effects were observed with similar proportions, n = 724 RS, 191 FS neurons; Figure 1E–H, Figure 1—source data 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figures 1E-H.

claim: The findings suggested that the MD impacts its PL targets in a manner distinct from those observed across sensory thalamocortical loops.
source: These findings suggested that, at least with this type of broad and sustained manipulation, the MD impacts its PL targets in a manner distinct from those observed across sensory thalamocortical loops, consistent with previous findings (Schmitt et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings, supported by a citation.

claim: BDA was iontophoretically delivered into the lateral MD or the ventral division of the MGB to anterogradely label small populations of axons.
source: To begin identifying whether the functional divergence observed across the MD→PL and MGB→A1 pathways may be partly explained by gross structural features (Casas-Torremocha et al., 2019; Rodriguez-Moreno et al., 2020), we anterogradely labeled small populations of axons originating from the lateral MD or the ventral division of the MGB. To this end, we iontophoretically delivered biotinylated dextran amine (BDA) into these areas (Figure 2A,D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1; see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used for anatomical tracing.

claim: There is a significant difference in thalamocortical bouton sizes across the MD→PL and MGB→A1 pathways, with MGB→A1 showing a significantly higher proportion of larger boutons in layer 4.
source: This procedure revealed a significant difference in thalamocortical bouton sizes across the MD→PL and MGB→A1 pathways, with the latter showing a significantly higher proportion of larger boutons in layer 4 (mean bouton projection areas: A1 (L4) = 1.28 ± 0.54 µm² vs. PL (L3) = 0.77 ± 0.42 µm²; p < 0.001, Kruksal Wallis test with Dunn's post hoc test, Figure 2—source data 2; p < 0.001, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test Figure 2G,H; Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative anatomical finding shown in Figure 2G,H.

claim: MD boutons in all layers of PL are significantly smaller than MGB boutons in layer 4 of A1.
source: We however noted that MD boutons in all layers of PL and in MGB boutons in layers 1, 3, and 5 of A1 are significantly smaller, than MGB boutons in layer 4 of A1.
evidence: This is a quantitative anatomical finding from the study.

claim: MGB boutons in layers 1, 3, and 5 of A1 are significantly smaller than MGB boutons in layer 4 of A1.
source: We however noted that MD boutons in all layers of PL and in MGB boutons in layers 1, 3, and 5 of A1 are significantly smaller, than MGB boutons in layer 4 of A1.
evidence: This is a quantitative anatomical finding from the study.

claim: The substantial difference in bouton size is consistent with the notion that the MGB→A1 is a driver pathway.
source: This substantial difference in bouton size is consistent with the notion that the MGB→A1 is a driver pathway (Casas-Torremocha et al., 2017; Viaene et al., 2011), whereas the MD→PL pathway may be better described as a modulatory one.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the anatomical findings, supported by citations.

claim: The MD→PL pathway may be better described as a modulatory pathway.
source: This substantial difference in bouton size is consistent with the notion that the MGB→A1 is a driver pathway (Casas-Torremocha et al., 2017; Viaene et al., 2011), whereas the MD→PL pathway may be better described as a modulatory one.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the anatomical findings.

claim: The MGB findings are consistent with previous studies using a comparable approach.
source: The MGB findings are also consistent with previous studies using a comparable approach (Viaene et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement compares the current findings to prior literature, supported by a citation.

claim: Trans-synaptic anterograde AAV was used to label postsynaptic targets of MD and MGB within the PL and A1 with cre-recombinase.
source: To examine additional structural sources of functional divergence across the MD→PL and MGB→A1 pathways, we took advantage of the recently characterized trans-synaptic anterograde adeno-associated virus (AAV) as a labeling tool (Zingg et al., 2017). Specifically, we used this tool to label, respectively postsynaptic targets of MD and MGB (thalamic injection sites, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) within the PL and A1 with cre-recombinase, followed by the injection of a second AAV harboring a pan-neuronal promoter driving cre-dependent expression of a fluorescent protein, mCherry (Figure 3A).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used for anatomical tracing, supported by a citation.

claim: Both experiments (MD→PL and MGB→A1) labeled comparable putative postsynaptic neurons across animals.
source: We performed this experiment across four mice for each system (MD→PL and MGB→A1). Although both experiments (MD→PL and MGB→A1) labeled comparable putative postsynaptic neurons across animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 2—source data 1), there were important differences in the spatial localization of these neurons.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the anatomical tracing experiment shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: MGB targeted A1 neurons were most densely localized to L4.
source: More specifically, while MGB targeted A1 neurons were most densely localized to L4, MD targeted PL neurons were more spatially diffuse (Figure 3C–E; n = 2 to 3 sections, N = 4 mice per condition, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is an anatomical finding from the study shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: MD targeted PL neurons were more spatially diffuse.

source: To address this question, we implemented the mammalian GFP reconstitution across synaptic partners (mGRASP) technique. This approach is based on functional complementation between two nonfluorescent GFP fragments that are localized to a pre- and postsynaptic pair, thereby specifically labeling the synapses between two targets for more accurate quantification (Feng et al., 2014).

claim: A two-step labeling approach using retrograde AAV and G-deleted pseudorabies was used to identify monosynaptic inputs innervating MD→PL neurons.
source: To further characterize the structural differences across the two thalamocortical loops, we sought to map the inputs of the MD→PL and MGB→A1 microcircuits with higher specificity. As such, and to precisely identify the set of monosynaptic inputs innervating MD→PL neurons, we used a two-step labeling approach. First, we rendered MD→PL neurons susceptible to monosynaptic rabies tracing by injecting a retrograde adeno-associated virus (AAVrg) harboring cre-recombinase (Tervo et al., 2016) into the PL and two helper AAV viruses, one of which is cre-dependent to achieve pathway specificity, directly into the MD. Second, and following 2 weeks of incubation, we injected G-deleted pseudorabies into the MD (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; see Materials and methods) (Chatterjee et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used for input tracing, supported by citations.

Visual inspection of these representative sections showed that the MD→PL population receives substantial projections from frontal cortical areas including the prelimbic, cingulate and secondary motor cortices (Figure 5A–C).

This analysis suggests that when compared on a single neuron basis MD→PL neurons receive five times as many cortical inputs relative to individual MGB→A1 neurons (Figure 7A,B, Figure 7—source data 1), while the opposite pattern holds for midbrain inputs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
